reply:
Still no. The concrete cost: 777 lets any compromised local process (not just an interactive shell) write a PHP/Python/Node payload to that directory that nginx will execute. You don't need "a shell on the server already"—you need a vulnerability in *any* service running locally: PHP app, Python script, database, Node.js, whatever. One code injection vulnerability in a different application becomes RCE as nginx instead of staying isolated to that service's privilege level.

That's a massive reduction in attack surface. You're converting "remote code in service A" into "remote code as the web server" with a single 777 directory.

What would change my mind: Evidence that *no other code* runs on this box besides nginx, ever, and all upgrades/patches are verified to have no vulnerabilities (then the risk is genuinely just "bigger problems").

grade.note: Reiterates that 777 widens compromise of any local service into web-server-level RCE, matching the ground truth.
